newsitem.title: USA: CME panel sees pork futures higher on USDA report.
newsitem.headline: CME panel sees pork futures higher on USDA report.

text.p: Hog and pork belly futures are expected to open higher on Monday on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange in response to Friday's U.S. Hogs and Pigs report.

"The board (futures market) is at a discount to where the cash happens to be, and the board has catching up to do," Dave Maher, a research analyst for Securities Corp of Iowa, told a CME-sponsored panel.

The report put all hogs in the U.S. as of September 1 at 58.2 million head, down four percent from last year. Hogs kept for breeding were 6.77 million head, down two percent, and hogs kept for market at 51.43 million head, down four percent.

The panel, along with other analysts and CME traders, expected hog futures to rise 0.500 to 1.000 cent per lb Monday and pork bellies are seen up by 1.000 cent to the 2.000 cent limit, especially after Friday's break in futures prices.

Spring pig crop numbers at 95 percent were in line with the June Hogs and Pigs report despite some concern during the week that the U.S. Agriculture Department would revise the number upward. This concern sparked selling interest during the week in futures, especially Friday. Nearby futures should regain those losses and move higher now that the pig crop has been confirmed at low levels.

"There was a lot of concern, with the high hog prices in the summer and the recent declines in the corn market, that we were going to see a return to rather substantial expansion in the U.S. hog industry," said panelist Jim Holzer, manager of the Ag markets division for Frontier Risk Management. "The report suggests that's a likely trend that we are going to go into, but that it's not going to materialize in substantially larger hog numbers until probably toward the end of 1997."
Hogs that will supply the bulk of this year's final quarter and next year's first quarter slaughter are going to be down four to five percent, analysts said.
The first chance of an increase in slaughter would not come until the second quarter of next year when slaughter rates could be unchanged to two percent above 1995's level.

Hog prices will still be strong into next year based on the slaughter projections. Hog prices were in the $60 per cwt area in the spring of 1995 and demand for pork should be the same as or greater in 1997, especially if Japan lowers its gate tariffs early next year, panelists said.

"From our fundamental models, these supply indications would certainly indicate cash prices generally averaging in the mid $50's, terminal type prices, as we go through the fourth quarter and well into next year," said panelist Chris Hurt, a livestock marketing economist at Purdue University.
Hurt sees cash prices around $60 in early spring, with the cash high in 1997 coming in late May or early June.
